name: picat
desc: Simple, and yet powerful, logic-based multi-paradigm programming language
why: A logic-based multi-paradigm language blending Prolog-style search with imperative features, unusual and worth an evening.

brief.what_it_is: Picat is a logic-based, multi-paradigm programming language for general-purpose work, built on pattern-matching rules that define predicates, functions, and actors. It takes Picat source programs, including scripts that read files, and runs them on its own virtual machine. It also supports constraint modeling through solver modules (cp, sat, mip, smt) and planning built on tabling. The homepage says it can be used for symbolic computation, scripting, and modeling tasks.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage presents Picat as a simple yet powerful language that mixes declarative features (explicit non-determinism, unification, functions, list comprehensions, constraints, tabling) with imperative ones (assignments, loops) so everyday programming stays practical. It claims to be more expressive and scalable than Prolog, and to suit problems that would otherwise need an imperative algorithm.
brief.how_it_works: Programs are sets of rules with pattern matching, which the homepage says lets the implementation index rules and run faster than Prolog. Tabling memoizes calls and answers, and mode declarations such as max on an argument let tabled search keep only the best answer; the homepage's Euler #67 example uses this to solve a 100-row triangle in 0.01 seconds. The implementation uses a well-designed virtual machine with a memory manager that garbage-collects and grows its stacks and data areas as needed.
brief.install_notes: The homepage text does not describe installation steps, hardware needs, or first-run configuration. It links to a Download section, which I did not follow. The Brew formula installs an executable named picat.
brief.standout: Picat puts explicit non-determinism, tabling with aggregate modes, and a common interface across several constraint solvers (cp, sat, mip, smt) into one language that also reads like a scripting language. Its example planner solves the Farmer's problem by tabling state transitions with best_plan rather than using a separate planner.
brief.status: Maintained. The homepage lists a Version 3.9#12 release dated 8/28/2026, competition results at XCSP'26 and MiniZinc'26, and a news feed with recent items, including a web-based IDE and editor integrations for IntelliJ, Emacs, VS Code, and Geany.
brief.caveats: Performance and expressiveness claims (order-of-magnitude fewer lines than Prolog, faster than Prolog through pattern-matching indexing) are the authors' own assertions on the homepage, not independent benchmarks. The homepage says nothing about supported platforms or the license beyond 'Picat can be used for any fair purpose, including commercial applications'. The homepage content came from the site's HTML text; I did not read the separate documentation pages.
quotes: Simple, and yet powerful, logic-based multi-paradigm programming language
Picat is a rule-based language, in which predicates, functions, and actors are defined with pattern-matching rules.
I think Picat is like a perfect Swiss army knife that you can do anything with.

judge.reason: Picat makes logic programming practical to explore, combining explicit search and tabling with constraint solvers in a general-purpose language.

entry.title: Picat
entry.tldr: A logic programming language that mixes Prolog-style search and unification with loops, assignments, tabling, and constraint solvers, so planning problems become short rule sets.
entry.deeper_look:
Picat is a general-purpose language built on pattern-matching rules. Predicates, functions, and actors are all defined with rules, and programs run on the language's own virtual machine. It can be used for scripting, symbolic computation, and modeling tasks.

It is a cousin of Prolog, and it keeps the declarative features: explicit non-determinism, unification, list comprehensions, constraints. It also adds assignments and loops, so ordinary programming does not require twisting a problem into logic. The homepage says pattern matching lets the implementation index rules and run faster than Prolog.

The idea underneath is tabling, which memoizes calls and answers. With a mode declaration such as `max` on an argument, a tabled search keeps only the best answer. The homepage's Euler #67 example uses this to solve a 100-row triangle in 0.01 seconds. The same mechanism drives planning: its Farmer's problem example tables state transitions and uses `best_plan` instead of a separate planner.

Picat also offers constraint modeling through several solver modules (cp, sat, mip, smt) behind a common interface. That makes it a place to try out the same puzzle on different solving engines without changing languages.

entry.whats_unique: Tabling with aggregate modes, explicit non-determinism, and a shared interface to the cp, sat, mip, and smt solvers sit in one language that also reads like a scripting language.
entry.caveats: The speed and brevity claims relative to Prolog are the authors' own, not independent benchmarks, and this entry is based on the homepage rather than the documentation.
